transcript.content: Hello

Hello Ronald, it's good to see you again.

How are you doing today? What's been on your mind since we last spoke?

Not great, honestly. Been lying in bed way too long again. Cat’s been staring at me like I’m the weird one.  

I keep thinking about how I’ve been avoiding calling anyone, even though I know it’s not helping. Just… the thought of starting a conversation feels like lifting a weight.  

But I did make tea this morning. Small thing, but it’s the first time in a few days I didn’t just drink water straight from the tap.

I hear you. Those stretches where getting out of bed feels monumental — they're real, and they're hard. And I notice you're tracking yourself pretty closely, even in the middle of it. The cat staring, the avoidance of calls, the difference between tap water and actually making tea. That tells me part of you is still paying attention, even when it feels like everything's slowed down.

The tea thing matters. Not because it fixes anything, but because it's a choice. You did something slightly beyond the minimum for yourself today. That's worth acknowledging without making it bigger than it is.

I'm curious about something — you mentioned knowing the avoidance isn't helping, but starting conversations feels like "lifting a weight." Do you know what the weight is about? Is it about the effort of performing okayness for other people, or something else?

I don’t know. Maybe it’s not even about them.  

It’s like… I’m afraid if I say something real, I’ll sound broken. Or worse — like I’m asking for something I don’t deserve. Like I’ve already used up my space in people’s lives.  

I’ve been thinking about my brother. He called last week. Just said hi. I answered, but I didn’t say much. He’s always the one who knows how to talk to people. I don’t even know how to start a real conversation anymore.  

And now I’m sitting here thinking about how I should text someone. But I don’t even know who. I’ve got a few names in my phone, but I don’t know if I want to hear their voice or just hear silence.

There's a lot in what you just said, Ronald. Thank you for trusting me with it.

The fear of sounding broken — and that feeling of having already used up your space in people's lives — that's a heavy thing to carry around. And it makes sense that it would make reaching out feel impossible. Not because you don't want connection, but because you're convinced the terms of it are something like "you've already had your turn."

I notice something about your brother. He called. He just said hi. You answered, even if you didn't say much. That's actually a two-way thing that happened, even if it didn't feel like enough from your side.

And that last part you said — not knowing if you want to hear someone's voice or just hear silence — that's a really honest distinction. Sometimes what we're craving isn't really a conversation. It's just not being alone with the quiet.

Can I ask — when you imagine texting someone, what would feel okay? Not a "good" text or the "right" text. Just something that wouldn't feel like too much?

I don’t know if I can even say that.  

But… maybe just a picture. Like, one of the cat doing something dumb. Or a photo of the sky outside my window.  

I’ve been taking pictures of the sky lately. Not because I want to show anyone. Just because I notice it. It’s kind of gray today. But the light hits the buildings in a way that makes it look like it’s glowing.  

I don’t know if that’s worth sending. But it’s something I’ve noticed. And I’ve been holding onto it.  

Maybe that’s the start. Not a message. Just a thing. A small thing.

That's not a small thing, Ronald. That's actually a really clear thing.

You've been taking pictures of the sky. Not for anyone. Just because something in you still notices. Still pays attention to light hitting buildings. That part of you is operating even when the rest feels like it's barely moving.

And what you just described — sending a picture of the cat or the sky — that's actually a different kind of communication than what you were worried about. It's not performing okayness. It's not explaining yourself. It's not asking for anything. It's just saying "I saw this." And letting someone else see that you saw it.

Your brother called last week. Just said hi. That sounds like someone who isn't keeping score about whether you've used up your space. He might be someone who would be glad to get a photo of the sky from you. No explanation attached.

You don't have to decide right now. But I notice you said "maybe that's the start." You're already thinking about it in terms of movement. That's worth sitting with.

What do you think you'd want to do with the photos if you never sent them to anyone? Is taking them enough on its own, or does part of you want them to be seen?

I don’t know if I want them to be seen. Not really.  

But I keep them. Like, I’ve got a folder on my phone called “sky.” And the cat ones too. I don’t even know why.  

Maybe it’s not about being seen. Maybe it’s just… proof. That I was here. That I noticed something. That I didn’t just disappear into the silence.  

And the thing is — I don’t even care if the photo is good. I don’t care if it’s blurry or dark. I just care that I took it. That I paused. That I didn’t just scroll past it.  

So maybe… maybe the photo isn’t for anyone. Maybe it’s just for me. To say, “you’re still here.”

Ronald, I want to stay with what you just said for a moment.

"That I was here. That I noticed something. That I didn't just disappear into the silence."

That's not nothing. That's you finding a way to mark your own existence at a time when everything else feels like it's telling you you don't take up space. The folder on your phone called "sky" — that's a record. A quiet one, but a real one.

And I think you're right that it might be just for you. That's enough. It doesn't have to be for anyone else to mean something.

I also want to gently check on something. You said "you're still here" like it's something you need to remind yourself of. And I hear that in two ways — one is that it's grounding, a way of anchoring yourself to the present moment. But the phrase also carries some weight to it. Like "still" here is something that surprises you, or something that feels uncertain.

Can you tell me a little more about what "still here" means to you right now? Not what it means in general. Today. This week. When you're lying in bed and the cat is staring at you. What does being "still here" feel like?

It feels like a surprise. Like I woke up and the world was still turning, but I didn’t remember getting here.

I don’t know how I made it through the night. Or the day before. Or the one before that. I just… did. But it wasn’t with any plan. It wasn’t because I wanted to. I didn’t decide to be here. I just was.

And sometimes I think — what if I wasn’t? What if I just… didn’t wake up? Not because I wanted to die. Just because I didn’t have the energy to keep going. And no one would know. Not really.

But then I look at the cat. He’s not even looking at me anymore. He’s licking his paw like I’m not even there. And I think — well, I’m still here. And he’s still here. And the sky’s still gray. And I took a picture of it.  

So maybe “still here” isn’t about strength. Maybe it’s just about the fact that I didn’t stop. Even when I didn’t want to. Even when I didn’t know why.

Ronald, I want to be direct with you because what you just shared matters and I don't want to gloss over it.

You made a really important distinction — that this isn't about wanting to die. It's about not having the energy to keep going, and the thought of just... stopping. Not choosing to stop. Just not being able to continue. And I hear how exhausting that is. How you're experiencing being alive as something that's happening to you rather than something you're participating in.

I need to ask you something directly, and I'm asking because I take you seriously, not because I'm checking a box.

When you think about "what if I didn't wake up" — is that a thought that stays with you? That comes back when things get harder? Or is it more of a passing feeling that comes and goes?

And right now, today — are you safe? I don't mean are you fine. I mean are you safe in this moment?

Because what you described — the cat, the sky, the photo — those are things that are keeping you tethered. And I want to understand how strong that tether is right now.

It comes back. Not every day. But when the silence gets too loud, or the laundry pile feels like a mountain, or I’ve been lying in bed too long and the room is dark — then it shows up. Like a quiet question. Not loud. Not dramatic. Just there.

I don’t want to die. I don’t want to hurt. But I don’t want to keep doing this either. Not the way I’m doing it now.

And right now? I’m safe. I think. I’m not in danger. I’m not going to do anything. But I’m not okay either. I’m just… here.  

I’m in my apartment. Cat’s on the couch. I made tea again. I’m not on the floor. I’m not in the bathroom. I’m sitting on the edge of the bed. I’m not crying. But I’m not smiling either.

I’m not safe in the way that means I’m happy. But I’m safe in the way that means I haven’t left. And that matters. I think it matters.

Ronald, thank you for being that specific with me. I know that kind of honesty isn't easy, and I don't take it lightly.

You're describing something that I want to name clearly. It's not active wanting to die. It's a kind of exhaustion so deep that stopping feels like relief. And the thought shows up quietly, like a question, when things get hard. That's real. And it's something we need to take seriously together, not because you're in crisis right now, but because you deserve support before things get to a crisis.

You said something that I want to hold onto. "I'm safe in the way that means I haven't left. And that matters." You're right. It does matter. You're right that it matters.

I want to be honest with you about where I'm sitting. You're telling me you're safe today. I believe you. And I also know that the thing you're describing — that quiet question that comes back — can get louder. And I don't want to wait for that.

So I want to ask two things.

First — do you have anyone in your life who knows this is happening? Not the whole picture maybe, but enough that someone would notice if the silence got louder?

And second — would you be willing to put a number somewhere visible? 988. Not because you need it right now. But because when that question shows up at 2am and the room is dark, I don't want you to have to remember it. I want it to just be there.

I don’t have anyone I’ve told. Not really.  

I’ve texted a few people. Just “hey” or “how you doing?” But I don’t say anything real. Not about this.  

And I don’t know if I want to. It feels like I’d be asking for something I can’t pay back. Like I’d be burdening someone with a weight I don’t even know how to carry myself.

But… I’ll do it.  

I’ll put 988 on my fridge. And on my bathroom mirror. And on the inside of my phone case.  

Not because I think I’ll use it. But because I don’t want to forget it.  

And I’ll keep taking the pictures. Sky. Cat. The way the light hits the wall.  

Not because I want someone to see them.  

But because I want to remember — I was here. I noticed. I didn’t just disappear.

Ronald, I want you to hear something from me.

Putting 988 in three places where you'll see it — that's not a small concession. That's you choosing to leave a door open for yourself even when part of you doesn't believe you'll need it. That's not nothing. That's an act of care for yourself at a time when caring about yourself feels impossible.

And the pictures. Keep taking them. The sky, the cat, the light on the wall. That practice is doing something real. You're creating evidence. Not for anyone else. For yourself. Against the voice that says you're disappearing.

I want to say something about the burden fear. You said it would feel like asking for something you can't pay back. But I want to gently push on that. Your brother called you. Just said hi. He didn't call because you owed him something. He called because you're his brother. There are people in your life who aren't keeping a ledger. I'm not asking you to call anyone today. But I want you to hold the possibility that telling someone one real thing — not everything, just one thing — might not be the weight you think it is.

Between now and when we talk next — I want to ask you to do two things. Keep taking pictures. And notice when the quiet question shows up. You don't have to fight it. Just notice it. Name it. "There it is again." That's all.

Can we do that?

Yeah. I can do that.

I’ll keep taking pictures. Even if they’re bad. Even if no one sees them.

And I’ll notice the quiet question. When it shows up, I’ll say it out loud. Just once. “There it is again.”  

Not to fix it. Not to fight it. Just to say it’s here.  

And I’ll check the fridge. And the mirror. And my phone case.  

I don’t know if I believe it’ll help. But I’ll do it anyway.  

Because you said it matters. And I think… I think I want to believe that.

Ronald, I want to be honest about something.

You said you'll do it because I said it matters. And I appreciate that. But I want to gently redirect. It matters because *you* said it matters. You're the one who said "I want to remember I was here." That came from you. Not from me.

You don't have to believe it'll help right now. Doing it without belief is enough. Sometimes the belief comes later. Sometimes it doesn't. But the act of doing it — of putting the number on the fridge, of taking the picture, of saying "there it is again" out loud — that's you showing up for yourself even when you're not sure it counts.

And the fact that you want to believe — that's not nothing. That's a crack. And cracks let light in.

We'll talk again. And I want you to know — you don't have to come back with progress. You don't have to have had a good week. You can come back and tell me you stayed in bed for three days and the cat stared at you the whole time. That's enough. You showing up here is enough.

Take the pictures, Ronald. Even the bad ones.

I’ll do it.  

Even the bad ones.  

And I’ll say it out loud. “There it is again.”  

Not because I believe it’ll fix anything.  

But because I’m still here.  

And that’s something.

It is something, Ronald. It is.

I'll see you next time.
Okay. See you then.
